title: The Impact of Financial Literacy on Personal Financial Management: An Empirical Study Among Young Adults
authors: Bhavana, K.S.; Sreelakshmi, M.R.; Surya, N.
venue: International Journal of Finance and Business Management Research
tldr: An empirical study of 300 young adults demonstrates that financial literacy significantly impacts savings behavior, budgeting practices, and investment decisions.
problem_and_motivation: Young adults in India face increasing financial complexity with multiple investment options, credit products, and digital payment systems. Despite this, many lack the financial literacy needed to make informed decisions. Understanding the specific impact of financial literacy on different aspects of personal finance is crucial for designing effective interventions.
approach: Surveyed 300 young adults aged 18-30 across urban and semi-urban areas in India.
Measured financial literacy across four dimensions: budgeting, saving, investing, and debt management.
Correlated literacy scores with financial behaviors and outcomes.
Applied regression analysis to identify the strongest predictors of financial behavior.
Compared findings across demographic groups including gender, education, and income levels.
Developed recommendations for financial education programs based on empirical findings.
findings: num: 300 young adults participated in the study.
num: 45% demonstrated high financial literacy across all four dimensions.
num: 38% demonstrated moderate literacy with knowledge gaps in investing.
num: Strong positive correlation (r=0.72) between literacy and savings behavior.
num: Moderate correlation (r=0.58) between literacy and budgeting practices.
num: 62% of high-literacy respondents had emergency savings, compared to 23% of low-literacy respondents.
num: 71% of high-literacy respondents actively invested, compared to 34% of low-literacy respondents.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This empirical study provides quantitative evidence on how financial literacy specifically impacts different aspects of personal finance among young adults. The finding that literacy has the strongest impact on savings behavior (r=0.72) followed by budgeting (r=0.58) suggests that financial education programs should prioritize these areas. The significant disparities between high and low literacy groups in emergency savings (62% vs 23%) and investment participation (71% vs 34%) demonstrate the practical importance of literacy.
directly_justifies: Financial literacy has a strong positive correlation with savings behavior (r=0.72).
Knowledge gaps in investing are the most common literacy deficit among young adults.
Significant disparities exist between high and low literacy groups in key financial behaviors.
limits: Cross-sectional design cannot establish causal relationships between literacy and behavior.
Indian context may limit generalizability to other countries.
Self-reported financial behaviors may introduce response bias.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: All 14 topic domains were systematically scanned. Domain 1 (Current Personal Finance Landscape) applies through 1.A (Current State) and 1.D (Behavioral Barriers). Domain 12 (Evaluation Frameworks) is highly relevant through 12.A (Financial Literacy and System Evaluation) and 12.B (User Satisfaction and Adoption). Other domains like 2-3, 4-11, 13-14 are less directly applicable as the paper focuses on measuring literacy impact rather than system design or technical implementation.

limitations: Cross-sectional design limits causal inference between literacy and behavior.
Indian context may not generalize to other economic and cultural settings.
Self-reported financial behavior measures may overestimate actual practices.
Study focuses on young adults (18-30); findings may not apply to other age groups.
